chengdu.name: Chengdu
chengdu.summary: The capital of Sichuan province and China's fourth most populous city, with over 20 million residents; founded in the 4th century BC, it is linked to giant pandas and Sichuan cuisine.

kung-pao-chicken.name: Kung Pao chicken
kung-pao-chicken.summary: Spicy stir-fried Sichuan dish made with chicken, peanuts, vegetables and chili peppers, whose popularity spread throughout China with many regional variations.

sichuan-pepper.name: Sichuan pepper
sichuan-pepper.summary: Spice made from the dried outer shell of Zanthoxylum fruit, used in Sichuan cuisine for a tingling, numbing effect, and unrelated to black or chili pepper despite the name.

taishan-guangdong.name: Taishan, Guangdong
taishan-guangdong.summary: A county-level city in Guangdong province, China, historically the origin of most Chinese immigrants to the United States before immigration was closed in 1924.

cantonese-cuisine.name: Cantonese cuisine
cantonese-cuisine.summary: The cuisine of Cantonese-speaking people from China's Guangdong province, one of China's Eight Great Traditions and, through emigration, the style behind most Chinese restaurants in the West until the late 20th century.

american-chinese-cuisine.name: American Chinese food
american-chinese-cuisine.summary: A style of Chinese cuisine developed by Chinese Americans and adapted to local tastes, often quite different from cooking styles in China itself.

lower-east-side.name: Lower East Side
lower-east-side.summary: Historically immigrant, working-class neighborhood in southeastern Manhattan that later underwent rapid gentrification beginning in the mid-2000s.

1931-china-floods.name: 1931 China Floods
1931-china-floods.summary: Catastrophic floods along the Yangtze and Huai rivers from June to August 1931, with death toll estimates ranging up to roughly two million.

william-chen-wing-young.name: William Wing Young
william-chen-wing-young.summary: William Chen Wing Young: Chinese-Australian businessman in Melbourne (1896–1974), known for inventing and popularising the dim sim, or 'dimmy', in the 1940s.

dim-sim.name: Dim sim
dim-sim.summary: Deep-fried, thick-skinned meat dumpling popular in Australia, inspired by Cantonese dim sum and popularised in the 1940s by Chinese-Australian William Wing Young.

expo-2010.name: Expo 2010
expo-2010.summary: A World Expo held in Shanghai in 2010 under the theme 'Better City – Better Life,' drawing over 73 million visitors and a record number of participating countries.

neo-chinese-style.name: Neo-Chinese style
neo-chinese-style.summary: A late 20th- and early 21st-century movement blending traditional Chinese elements with modern design in architecture, interiors and fashion, popular among younger Chinese in the 2020s.

he-jingtang.name: He Jingtang
he-jingtang.summary: Chinese architect, born 1938, whose works include Olympic venues for Beijing 2008, the China Pavilion at Expo 2010, and the University of Macau's new campus.

dougong.name: Dougong
dougong.summary: A system of interlocking wooden brackets in traditional Chinese architecture, used since the Zhou dynasty to join pillars to roof frames without glue or fasteners.

ding-vessel.name: ding
ding-vessel.summary: Ancient Chinese ritual bronze cauldrons standing on legs, used for cooking, storage and offerings; owning them became a symbol of royal authority under the Zhou dynasty.

china-art-museum-shanghai.name: China Art Museum, Shanghai
china-art-museum-shanghai.summary: A municipal art museum of Shanghai, housed in the former China Pavilion building from Expo 2010; it succeeded the earlier Shanghai Art Museum, founded in 1956.

nanjing-road.name: West Nanjing Road
nanjing-road.summary: The western section of Shanghai's main shopping street, formerly known as Bubbling Well Road before joining the historic Nanjing Road.

shanghai-race-club.name: Shanghai Race Club
shanghai-race-club.summary: A Shanghai horse-racing club established in 1850 and based at the Shanghai Racecourse, whose activities ended after the Communist takeover placed it under military administration in 1951.

people-s-square-shanghai.name: People's Square
people-s-square-shanghai.summary: A large public square in Shanghai's Huangpu District, site of the city's municipal government headquarters and the reference point for measuring highway distances.

shanghai-library.name: Shanghai Library
shanghai-library.summary: A major public library in Shanghai founded in 1952, now one of the largest libraries in the world with 58 million volumes housed in a 24-story main building.

power-station-of-art.name: Power Station of Art
power-station-of-art.summary: China's first state-owned contemporary art museum, in Shanghai, built at the former site of the Nanshi Electric Plant and opened in 2012; it hosts the Shanghai Biennale.

mandarin-collar.name: Mandarin collar
mandarin-collar.summary: A short, stand-up shirt or jacket collar named for the Qing-era Chinese officials who wore it as part of their uniform.

socialist-realism.name: Socialist realism
socialist-realism.summary: The official art style of the Soviet Union and other socialist states, using idealized, photorealistic scenes to advance the socialist cause; proclaimed doctrine in 1934.

second-sino-japanese-war.name: Second Sino-Japanese War
second-sino-japanese-war.summary: A war between China and Japan from 1937 to 1945, regarded as the start of World War II in Asia, and the largest Asian war of the 20th century.

kuomintang.name: Kuomintang
kuomintang.summary: Major Chinese political party founded by Sun Yat-sen in 1894, the sole ruling party of China from 1928 to 1949 before retreating to Taiwan after losing the Chinese Civil War.

chinese-civil-war.name: Chinese Civil War
chinese-civil-war.summary: A conflict between the Nationalist Kuomintang and the Chinese Communist Party fought mostly from 1927 to 1949, paused during the Japanese invasion, and ending with the Communists' victory and the Kuomintang's retreat to Taiwan.

sino-indian-war.name: Sino-Indian War
sino-indian-war.summary: A 1962 border war between China and India fought in the North-East Frontier Agency and Aksai Chin regions over unresolved territorial claims.

north-east-frontier-agency.name: North-East Frontier Agency
north-east-frontier-agency.summary: Political division of British India and later India, administered from Shillong; reorganised from earlier frontier tracts in 1954 and replaced by Arunachal Pradesh in 1972.

aksai-chin.name: Aksai Chin
aksai-chin.summary: A region administered by China as part of Xinjiang and Tibet, forming the easternmost part of Kashmir and disputed with India since 1959.

ardagh-johnson-line.name: Johnson Line
ardagh-johnson-line.summary: A boundary line for Kashmir's northeastern frontier drawn by surveyor William Johnson and recommended by John Charles Ardagh, recognised by India but not by China in the Aksai Chin dispute.

mcmahon-line.name: McMahon Line
mcmahon-line.summary: The 1914 boundary between British India and Tibet set at the Simla Convention, still forming the de facto China-India border today, though its legal status remains disputed by China.

chiang-kai-shek.name: Chiang Kai-shek
chiang-kai-shek.summary: Chinese military and political leader (1887–1975) who headed the Nationalist government, fought Japan in World War II, and later led the Republic of China from Taiwan after losing the civil war.

long-march.name: Long March
long-march.summary: A 1934–1935 retreat of about 100,000 Chinese Communist troops from Kuomintang forces over roughly 10,000 kilometers, of whom only about 8,000 survived.

second-united-front.name: Second United Front
second-united-front.summary: An alliance between China's Nationalist and Communist parties to resist Japan's invasion during the Second Sino-Japanese War, suspending their civil war from 1937 to 1945.

xi-an-incident.name: Xi'an Incident
xi-an-incident.summary: A December 1936 crisis in which generals seized Chiang Kai-shek in Xi'an to force an end to the civil war against the Communists, leading to a Second United Front against Japan.

1959-tibetan-uprising.name: 1959 Tibetan Uprising
1959-tibetan-uprising.summary: Ten days of protests in Lhasa in March 1959 against Chinese rule, crushed by China's army; the Dalai Lama fled to India as a result.

14th-dalai-lama.name: 14th Dalai Lama
14th-dalai-lama.summary: Born 1935 and recognized in 1939 as the 14th Dalai Lama, Tibet's spiritual and former temporal leader, who has led the Tibetan government in exile since 1959.

battle-of-the-paracel-islands.name: Battle of the Paracel Islands
battle-of-the-paracel-islands.summary: A naval battle on 19 to 20 January 1974 in which China defeated South Vietnam's navy, gaining full control of the Paracel Islands late in the Vietnam War.

sikkim.name: Sikkim
sikkim.summary: A small state in northeast India in the Eastern Himalaya, once an independent kingdom ruled by Buddhist priest-kings before becoming part of India in 1975.

nathu-la-and-cho-la-clashes.name: Nathu La and Cho La clashes
nathu-la-and-cho-la-clashes.summary: A series of 1967 border clashes between China and India near Sikkim, in which Indian forces held their ground and pushed back the Chinese troops.
nathu-la-and-cho-la-clashes.source_title: Nathu La and Cho La clashes

sm-u-65-germany.name: SM U-65
sm-u-65-germany.summary: A German submarine, one of 329 in the Imperial German Navy during World War I, that fought in the First Battle of the Atlantic.

ss-athos.name: SS Athos
ss-athos.summary: A French cargo-passenger ship, launched in 1914, that was sunk in the Mediterranean by a German submarine during World War I.

lu-xun.name: Lu Xun
lu-xun.summary: Chinese writer (1881–1936), pen name of Zhou Shuren, a leading figure of modern Chinese literature known for pioneering vernacular fiction and sharp, satirical essays.

classical-chinese.name: Literary Chinese
classical-chinese.summary: The written literary form of Chinese used from the 5th century BCE and adopted across Vietnam, Korea, Japan and the Ryukyus as a shared language of scholarship and administration until the early 20th century.

gao-xingjian.name: Gao Xingjian
gao-xingjian.summary: A Chinese-born, later French, novelist and playwright awarded the 2000 Nobel Prize in Literature, whose absurdist, avant-garde plays were often banned in China.

mo-yan.name: Mo Yan
mo-yan.summary: Chinese writer known for the 1986 novel Red Sorghum, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2012 for work blending folk tales, history and the contemporary.

ba-jin.name: Ba Jin
ba-jin.summary: Pen name of Li Yaotang (1904–2005), a Chinese anarchist writer and translator who wrote The Family and had a major impact on Chinese literature.

dream-of-the-red-chamber.name: Dream of the Red Chamber
dream-of-the-red-chamber.summary: An 18th-century Chinese novel by Cao Xueqin, one of the Four Great Classic Novels, noted for its psychological depth and its portrayal of a family's rise and decline.

mao-dun.name: Mao Dun
mao-dun.summary: Pen name of Shen Dehong (1896–1981), a Chinese novelist and founding member of the Chinese Communist Party celebrated for realist novels such as Midnight.

league-of-left-wing-writers.name: League of Left-Wing Writers
league-of-left-wing-writers.summary: A Chinese literary organization founded in Shanghai in 1930 that grew from over 50 to more than 400 members, many also Communist Party members, organized secretly in small cells.

guo-moruo.name: Guo Moruo
guo-moruo.summary: A Chinese author, poet, historian and official (1892–1978), prominent in the May Fourth Movement, who was persecuted in the Cultural Revolution but regained prominence in the 1970s.

lao-she.name: Lao She
lao-she.summary: Pen name of Shu Qingchun (1899–1966), a Chinese writer of Manchu ethnicity known for vivid portrayals of Beijing life, including the novel Rickshaw Boy; persecuted during the Cultural Revolution, he drowned himself or was murdered.

jinjiang-literature-city.name: Jinjiang Literature City
jinjiang-literature-city.summary: China's largest publisher of women's web fiction and an online forum based in Beijing, best known as a platform for original danmei novels.

ivan-turgenev.name: Ivan Turgenev
ivan-turgenev.summary: A Russian novelist, short story writer, poet and playwright (1818–1883); his story collection A Sportsman's Sketches (1852) and novel Fathers and Sons (1862) are landmarks of 19th-century Russian fiction.

cao-wenxuan.name: Cao Wenxuan
cao-wenxuan.summary: A Chinese novelist (born January 1954) best known for children's literature, who serves as vice president of the Beijing Writers Association and as a professor at Peking University; his novels have been translated into many languages.

hans-christian-andersen-award.name: Hans Christian Andersen Award
hans-christian-andersen-award.summary: A pair of biennial prizes from the International Board on Books for Young People, honoring a living children's author and illustrator with a gold medal bearing Andersen's bust; the writing award began in 1956, the illustration award in 1966.

shanda.name: Shanda
shanda.summary: A company founded in 1999 as Shanda Interactive Entertainment, which became China's largest online game company and had a landmark 2004 Nasdaq listing before later diversifying and going private.

chinese-academy-of-sciences.name: Chinese Academy of Sciences
chinese-academy-of-sciences.summary: China's national academy for the natural sciences, the world's largest research organization, with roots in the Republican-era Academia Sinica; it also founded companies such as Lenovo.

scimago-institutions-rankings.name: SCImago Institutions Rankings
scimago-institutions-rankings.summary: An international ranking of research institutions published since 2009 by a Spain-based research group, covering government, health, higher education, and other sectors.

academia-sinica.name: Academia Sinica
academia-sinica.summary: Taiwan's national academy, founded in Nanjing in 1928 and re-established in Taiwan in 1949, conducting research across sciences and humanities.

project-596.name: Project 596
project-596.summary: China's first nuclear weapons test, detonated on 16 October 1964 at Lop Nur, making China the world's fifth nuclear-armed state.

863-program.name: 863 Program
863-program.summary: A Chinese government program launched in 1986 to fund advanced technology development and reduce reliance on foreign technology, inspired by the US Strategic Defense Initiative.

global-innovation-index.name: Global Innovation Index
global-innovation-index.summary: An annual ranking of countries by their capacity for innovation, published since 2007 by the World Intellectual Property Organization using data from sources such as the World Bank.

joseph-needham.name: Joseph Needham
joseph-needham.summary: British biochemist, historian of science and sinologist known for the multivolume Science and Civilisation in China and for posing the "Needham Question" about China's loss of scientific leadership.

science-and-civilisation-in-china.name: Science and Civilisation in China
science-and-civilisation-in-china.summary: Ongoing book series begun in 1954 by historian Joseph Needham surveying the history of Chinese science and technology, credited with challenging Eurocentric views of scientific progress.

sugon.name: Sugon
sugon.summary: A Chinese supercomputer manufacturer, officially Dawning Information Industry Company, spun off from research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

wang-ling-historian.name: Wang Ling
wang-ling-historian.summary: A Chinese historian and sinologist (1918–1994) best known for his long collaboration with Joseph Needham on the history of science and technology in China.

needham-research-institute.name: Needham Research Institute
needham-research-institute.summary: A Cambridge research centre for the history of East Asian science and medicine, founded in 1968 and named for historian Joseph Needham.

university-of-science-and-technology-of-.name: University of Science and Technology of China
university-of-science-and-technology-of-.summary: A public research university in Hefei, China, founded in Beijing in 1958 by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and later relocated during the Cultural Revolution.
university-of-science-and-technology-of-.source_title: University of Science and Technology of China

university-of-the-chinese-academy-of-sci.name: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences
university-of-the-chinese-academy-of-sci.summary: A public university in Beijing owned by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, founded in 1978 as China's first graduate school and made an independent university in 2012.
university-of-the-chinese-academy-of-sci.source_title: University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences

mao-zedong.name: Mao Zedong
mao-zedong.summary: Chinese communist revolutionary who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and led it as Communist Party chairman until his death in 1976.

century-of-humiliation.name: Century of humiliation
century-of-humiliation.summary: A Chinese historiographical concept for the period from the First Opium War (1839–1842) to the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, marked by foreign domination and territorial losses under the Qing dynasty.

hainan-island-incident.name: Hainan Island Incident
hainan-island-incident.summary: A ten-day 2001 standoff between the US and China after a mid-air collision between a US Navy spy plane and a Chinese fighter jet near Hainan Island, resolved through careful diplomacy.

2008-summer-olympics-torch-relay.name: 2008 Olympic Torch Relay Protests
2008-summer-olympics-torch-relay.summary: Protests over Tibet and human rights that disrupted the 2008 Beijing Olympics torch relay in cities across North America and Europe, at times forcing its route to be changed or shortened.

puyi.name: Puyi
puyi.summary: Last emperor of China, reigning as the Xuantong Emperor of the Qing dynasty (1908–1912, briefly restored in 1917), later installed as puppet ruler of Japanese-controlled Manchukuo and held as a war criminal after World War II.

manchu-restoration.name: Manchu Restoration
manchu-restoration.summary: A failed 1917 attempt led by general Zhang Xun to restore the Chinese monarchy, briefly reinstating deposed Qing emperor Puyi for less than two weeks before Republican troops reversed it.

yuan-shikai.name: Yuan Shikai
yuan-shikai.summary: A Chinese general and statesman (1859–1916) who secured the Qing abdication, became the Republic of China's first formal president, and briefly declared himself emperor in 1915.

twenty-one-demands.name: Twenty-One Demands
twenty-one-demands.summary: A secret set of demands Japan made to China in 1915 seeking greatly expanded control, which sparked Chinese protests and a boycott and damaged Japan's standing with Britain and the US.

manchuria.name: Manchuria
manchuria.summary: A historical region of Northeast Asia covering present-day Northeast China and parts of the Russian Far East, the homeland of the Manchu people who founded the Qing dynasty.

duan-qirui.name: Duan Qirui
duan-qirui.summary: A Chinese general and statesman (1865–1936) who served as premier four times and controlled the Beijing government in the late 1910s as founder of the Anhui warlord clique.

mukden-incident.name: Mukden incident
mukden-incident.summary: A staged 1931 explosion used by Japanese military personnel as a pretext to invade Manchuria, leading to the puppet state of Manchukuo.

manchukuo.name: Manchukuo
manchukuo.summary: A Japanese puppet state set up in Manchuria in 1932, nominally ruled by former Chinese emperor Puyi but with all real decisions made by Japanese officials, lasting until 1945.

unequal-treaties.name: Unequal treaties
unequal-treaties.summary: Agreements imposed on East Asian countries such as Qing China, Japan and Korea by Western and Japanese imperial powers in the 19th and early 20th centuries, often after military defeat, forcing concessions like ceded territory and reduced tariff control.

guangxi-massacre.name: Guangxi Massacre
guangxi-massacre.summary: A series of lynchings, massacres and documented cases of cannibalism in Guangxi province during China's Cultural Revolution, 1967-1968, with an official death toll exceeding 100,000.

zheng-yi-writer.name: Zheng Yi
zheng-yi-writer.summary: Chinese writer (born 1947) of scar literature known for works like Old Well and Scarlet Memorial, who emigrated after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown.

scarlet-memorial.name: Scarlet Memorial
scarlet-memorial.summary: 1993 book of reportage by Chinese novelist Zheng Yi describing factional violence and cannibalism during the Cultural Revolution's Guangxi Massacre, praised for exposing Mao's regime.

emperor-yao.name: Emperor Yao
emperor-yao.summary: Legendary Chinese ruler traditionally dated to around 2356–2255 BCE, regarded by some sources as one of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.

emperor-shun.name: Emperor Shun
emperor-shun.summary: Legendary leader of ancient China's Youyu clan, regarded as one of the Five Emperors and praised by later Confucian philosophers for his modesty and filial piety.

five-races-under-one-union.name: Five Races Under One Union
five-races-under-one-union.summary: A founding principle of the Republic of China after 1911, holding that the Han, Manchu, Mongol, Hui and Tibetan peoples should coexist harmoniously within one nation.

ma-junwu.name: Ma Junwu
ma-junwu.summary: Scientist and educator in China, and the first president of Guangxi University, who lived from 1881 to 1940.

charles-darwin.name: Charles Darwin
charles-darwin.summary: English naturalist and biologist (1809-1882) known for his theory of evolution by natural selection, described as one of history's most influential figures.

maoism.name: Maoism
maoism.summary: Mao Zedong's adaptation of Marxism–Leninism for pre-industrial societies, which became the dominant ideology of the Chinese Communist Party from the 1950s until the late 1970s.

dialectical-materialism.name: Dialectical materialism
dialectical-materialism.summary: A philosophy developed from the writings of Friedrich Engels, combining Hegel's dialectic with materialism, holding that reality develops through internal contradictions; it became the Soviet Union's official philosophy.

china-family-panel-studies.name: China Family Panel Studies
china-family-panel-studies.summary: A biennial nationwide social survey launched in 2010 by Peking University to track changes in Chinese society, economy, education and health.

mark-mitin.name: Mark Mitin
mark-mitin.summary: Soviet Marxist–Leninist philosopher and Moscow State University professor (1901–1987) who focused on dialectical and historical materialism and criticism of bourgeois philosophy.

li-da-philosopher.name: Li Da
li-da-philosopher.summary: Early Chinese Marxist philosopher (1890-1966) and founding member of the Chinese Communist Party, who translated Marxist literature and spread Orthodox Marxism in China.

ai-siqi.name: Ai Siqi
ai-siqi.summary: Chinese Marxist philosopher and writer of Persian descent (1910–1966) who, after the founding of the People's Republic of China, served as Deputy Minister of Yunnan's Provincial Military and Political Department and Director of its Department of Justice.

reform-and-opening-up.name: Dengist reforms
reform-and-opening-up.summary: Economic reforms launched by the Chinese Communist Party in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, transforming China's planned economy toward what is now called a socialist market economy.

marxist-humanism.name: Marxist humanism
marxist-humanism.summary: A philosophical and political movement, emerging in 1932, that interprets Karl Marx's work through a humanist lens focused on human nature and flourishing.

one-divides-into-two.name: One Divides into Two
one-divides-into-two.summary: 1964 Chinese ideological debate over the nature of contradiction, rooted in Lenin's writings, in which Maoists attacked philosopher Yang Xianzhen's rival idea of 'Two Unites into One.'

may-fourth-movement.name: May Fourth Movement
may-fourth-movement.summary: 1919 student protests in Beijing against China's weak response to the Treaty of Versailles awarding Japan former German territory in Shandong, sparking nationalist mobilization and a broader New Culture Movement against traditional Confucian values.

great-leap-forward.name: Great Leap Forward
great-leap-forward.summary: A 1958 to 1962 Chinese industrialization campaign under Mao Zedong that forced rapid collectivization and caused a famine killing an estimated 15 to 55 million people.

chinese-folk-religion.name: Chinese folk religion
chinese-folk-religion.summary: Traditional Chinese religious practices honoring spirits, ancestors and deities, blended by the Song dynasty with Buddhist, Confucian and Taoist teachings; the government treats it as cultural heritage rather than an official religion.

mazu.name: Mazu
mazu.summary: A Chinese sea goddess, the deified form of a 10th-century Fujianese shamaness, widely worshipped by coastal Chinese and Taiwanese communities as a protector of seafarers.

yellow-emperor.name: Yellow Emperor
yellow-emperor.summary: A legendary Chinese sovereign and culture hero, traditionally credited with inventing the calendar, writing, boats and other innovations, and revered in Chinese folk religion as a deity.

dragon-king.name: Dragon King
dragon-king.summary: A celestial water and weather deity in Asian mythology, regarded as ruler of the seas and rivers and known by different names across cultures, such as Ryū in Japan.

pangu.name: Pangu
pangu.summary: A primordial being in Chinese mythology and Taoism said to have separated heaven and earth, his body later forming mountains and rivers.

caishen.name: Caishen
caishen.summary: A Chinese folk religion and Taoist god of wealth, often invoked during Chinese New Year and depicted riding a black tiger.

harbin.name: Harbin
harbin.summary: Capital of Heilongjiang province in northeastern China, founded in 1898 with the Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway and once home to a large Russian immigrant community.

list-of-celestial-masters.name: Celestial Master
list-of-celestial-masters.summary: Title of the hereditary leader of Zhengyi Taoism, continuing the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice, sometimes called the 'Taoist Pope' in English.

zhengyi-dao.name: Zhengyi Dao
zhengyi-dao.summary: A Chinese Taoist movement, also called the Way of Orthodox Unity, tracing its lineage to the Way of the Celestial Masters and today one of Daoism's two main denominations.
